title: The ENTIRE History of France in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of France in 10 Minutes
description:
From Gaul to the guillotine to the Eiffel Tower, this is the whole story of France in about ten minutes: Julius Caesar and the Gauls, Clovis and the Franks, Charlemagne, the 116-year Hundred Years' War, Joan of Arc, the Sun King and Versailles, the Bastille and the French Revolution, Napoleon and Waterloo, and how modern France was born. Every fact is checked.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #france #frenchhistory #napoleon #animatedhistory

beats.say: July 14th, 1789. An angry crowd in Paris is about to storm a feared royal prison: the Bastille.
Tear it down! Free the prisoners!
All seven of them?
Yep. Seven. Four forgers, two mentally ill men, and one nobleman locked up at his own family's request.
What the crowd really wanted was the gunpowder stored inside. By the end of the day, the fortress was theirs.
That day lit the fuse on a revolution. It would end with a king losing his head and a general named Napoleon running Europe.
But how did France get here? For that, we need to go way, way back.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of France in 10 Minutes
show.sub: From Gauls to Napoleon, and beyond

beats.say: Two thousand years ago, France wasn't France. It was Gaul, home to Celtic tribes called the Gauls.
Then Julius Caesar, a famous Roman general, conquered Gaul in the 50s BC.
For about five hundred years, Gaul was Roman. The Gauls picked up Roman roads, baths and Latin.
Over the centuries, their everyday Latin slowly turned into French.
When Rome's western empire collapsed in 476, Germanic tribes moved in. The most successful were the Franks.
In 486, Clovis, a Frankish king of about twenty, beat the last Roman ruler in Gaul.
Around the year 500, Clovis was baptized as a Christian, and many of his warriors followed him.
He made Paris his capital. And this new land of the Franks, Francia, is where the name France comes from.
Three hundred years later, the Franks got a superstar: Charlemagne, which means Charles the Great.
He fought war after war, and built an empire across what's now France, Germany and northern Italy.
On Christmas Day in the year 800, the Pope crowned him emperor in Rome.
But here's the twist. The most powerful man in Europe couldn't really write.
Einhard! How do you write the letter K again?
Sire, it is the middle of the night.
That skit is our joke, but Einhard really wrote that Charlemagne kept writing tablets under his pillow to practice.
He started too late in life, though, and never got very good.
Years after he died, his grandsons fought over the empire and split it three ways in 843. The western piece grew into France.
Jump to 1328. The French king died with no son, and the king of England saw his chance.
Edward the Third said his mother was the dead king's sister, so the French crown was his. France said no way.
In 1337, the fighting started. Historians later named it the Hundred Years' War, but they were bad at math.

show.label: The Hundred Years' War really lasted

beats.say: It wasn't nonstop. There were truces, the Black Death, and English archers winning huge battles like Agincourt in 1415.
By the 1420s, England and its French allies controlled Paris and most of the north. Then they surrounded Orléans.
Then a teenage farm girl named Joan came forward. She said the voices of saints told her to save France.
Give me soldiers, and I'll free Orléans.

tag.text: Charles, heir to the French throne

beats.say: You're seventeen, and you've never been in a battle.
Then I'd better start.
Charles said yes. About nine days after Joan arrived, the English gave up the siege of Orléans.
That summer, Charles was crowned king at Reims, with Joan standing right there.
But in 1430 she was captured and handed to the English, who put her on trial for heresy, meaning going against church teaching.
The judges asked her a trick question: was she in God's grace? Her answer stunned the court.
She said: if I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me so.

show.text: If I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God so keep me.
show.who: Joan of Arc, at her trial in Rouen, 1431 (trial record)

beats.say: She was still found guilty. In 1431, at about nineteen, she was burned at the stake. A new trial cleared her name twenty-five years later.
Her side won the war anyway. By 1453, the English had lost everything in France except the port of Calais.
France came out of the Middle Ages as one of Europe's strongest kingdoms.
In 1643, a four-year-old boy became king: Louis the Fourteenth.
He picked the sun as his symbol, and he became known as the Sun King. Everything was supposed to revolve around him.
In 1682 he moved his whole court to Versailles, an old hunting lodge he'd turned into a gigantic palace outside Paris.
Its Hall of Mirrors had three hundred fifty-seven mirrors. Perfect for a king who liked looking at himself.

show.label: Mirrors in the Hall of Mirrors

beats.say: Why move? He wanted France's powerful nobles close, where he could keep an eye on them.
Nobles even competed for the honor of helping him get dressed in the morning.
Your Majesty, may I have the honor of handing you your shirt?
Back off! It's my turn to hand him the shirt!
Gentlemen. The king is cold.
Louis ruled for seventy-two years and one hundred ten days. That's the longest reign of any major European king.
But he loved expensive wars. When he died in 1715, France was deep in debt.
By 1789, the king was Louis the Sixteenth, and France was broke.
France had borrowed huge sums for wars, including helping the Americans win their independence from Britain.
Then bad harvests sent bread prices soaring. Poor families spent most of their money just on bread.
Louis called a big national meeting to raise taxes. Instead, the commoners declared they were the real voice of the nation.
After the Bastille fell, the new Assembly declared that men are born free and equal in rights.
And there's no evidence Queen Marie Antoinette ever said let them eat cake. The writer Rousseau wrote that line down when she was a nine-year-old girl in Austria.
In 1792 France got rid of its king and became a republic. In January 1793, Louis was executed with the guillotine.
Then came the Reign of Terror. In about a year, roughly seventeen thousand people were officially executed as enemies of the Revolution.
In 1794, even Robespierre, the man most linked to the Terror, ended up on the guillotine himself.
The Revolution also tried ten-day weeks and clocks with ten hours a day. People hated them. But one idea stuck: the metric system.
All this chaos was perfect for a young general from the island of Corsica: Napoleon Bonaparte.
In 1799 he grabbed power in a coup, a takeover by force.
In 1804, he was crowned emperor in Notre-Dame cathedral in Paris, with the Pope right there.
So, I'll just place the crown on your...
Thanks. I'll take it from here.
He really did crown himself. It looks rude, but it wasn't a snub: the plan was agreed before the ceremony.
He also created the Napoleonic Code, one clear set of laws for all of France. It inspired laws in many countries.
And no, he wasn't short. He was about five foot seven, normal for his time. British cartoonists drew him tiny.
His armies conquered much of Europe. Then in 1812 he invaded Russia with a gigantic army, and most of it never came back.
In 1814 he was exiled to Elba, a tiny island off Italy. In 1815 he escaped, took back France, and lasted about a hundred days.
On June 18th, 1815, Britain's Duke of Wellington and the Prussian army beat him at Waterloo, in what's now Belgium.
This time, he was shipped to Saint Helena, a speck of an island far out in the South Atlantic. He died there in 1821.
After Napoleon, France couldn't make up its mind. It had kings again, revolutions in 1830 and 1848, then Napoleon's nephew as emperor.
In 1870 it became a republic again, and mostly stayed one.
For the 1889 World's Fair, Gustave Eiffel's company built a giant iron tower in Paris. It only had a permit for twenty years.
It was saved mainly because it made a great radio antenna.
Then came two world wars. In the first, French soldiers held the trenches for four long years.
In the second, Germany conquered France in just six weeks in 1940.
A general named Charles de Gaulle kept fighting from London. Later, in 1958, he founded the Fifth Republic, the system France still uses.
He's often quoted with one famous line about how hard France is to run:

show.text: How can you govern a country which has two hundred and forty-six varieties of cheese?
show.who: Charles de Gaulle, as quoted by Ernest Mignon in Les Mots du Général (1962)

beats.say: France used the guillotine until 1977, and it banned the death penalty in 1981.
So that's France. Gauls, Franks, a sun king, a revolution, an emperor, and a whole lot of cheese.
